power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Thirty-one right-handed adults (25 female, aged 18-42 years, M ± SD = 23.26 ± 5.34) with normal hearing and reading abilities were recruited. The final number of participants involved in the present study exceeded the a priori sample size (N = 28) estimated by means of a power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2009; repeated-measures ANOVA, within-factors, f = 0.25, α = 0.05, 1-β = 0.80, 3 measurements, correlation among repeated measures = 0.50). Additional participants were recruited to account for potential signal noise and data loss common in physiological recordings. Two participants were excluded from all analyses due to data recording failures (N = 29). An additional three participants were excluded specifically from the linguistic analyses due to missing audio recordings (N = 26).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. stat_check.summary_text: 1 possible error in t-tests or F-tests

table.text: Even after accounting for these speech dynamics, the Creativity contrast (C1) remained significant (β = 0.155, 95% CI [0.04, 0.27], t(542) = 2.537, p = .012).
Notably, controlling for speech dynamics removed the effect of C1 on error (p = .199), whereas the precision benefit of C2 remained (β = -0.166, 95% CI [-0.31, -0.02], t(547) = -2.189, p = .029).
Crucially, C1 maintained an independent direct effect on prospective overproduction (β = 0.164, 95% CI [0.04, 0.28], t(538) = 2.681, p = .008; R²marginal = 0.268, R²conditional = 0.539).

For absolute proportional error, speech dynamics dominated (both pFDR < .001), while semantic range was not significant (pFDR = 0.973), with the precision-enhancing effect of unconventionality remaining intact (C2: β = -0.207, 95% CI [-0.36, -0.05], t(548) = -2.650, p = .008).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Creative engagement is associated with distorted experiences of time, yet the cognitive basis remains unknown.
In particular, it is unclear how balancing broad associative exploration with task-relevant constraints during idea generation shapes prospective duration perception and subjective passage of time.
Here, 31 participants generated spoken sentences from prompt word triplets under conventional, creative, or unconventional instructions while producing target intervals (10 or 20 s).
Electrodermal activity and cardiac photoplethysmography were recorded throughout.
After each trial, participants completed ratings assessing their subjective temporal accuracy and passage of time.

Results showed that creative generation was characterized by broader within-response semantic range and reduced contextual uncertainty, reflecting a balance between conceptual divergence and structural coherence.
Creativity was also associated with greater temporal overproduction and absolute proportional error, whereas unconventionality improved temporal precision without a directional bias.
The coefficient of variation showed no significant condition effect, indicating no detectable differences in relative trial-to-trial variability.

Exploratory multilevel mediation revealed an indirect association between semantic range and temporal overproduction through speech duration, implicating verbal production dynamics in the relationship between semantic exploration and timing.
Subjective passage of time was faster in creative and unconventional conditions compared to conventional, dissociating subjective temporal experience from prospective interval production.
Physiologically, creative generation reduced phasic electrodermal activity, whereas unconventionality increased tonic skin conductance.
Across trials, higher heart rate and phasic electrodermal activity were associated with shorter produced intervals.
Overall, these findings reveal that temporal experience during creative thought reflects distinct contributions from embodied speech production dynamics and internal autonomic pacing.
Creative generation depends on the ability to move beyond dominant ideas while maintaining relevance to the current goal (Abraham, 2018; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Sawyer & Henriksen, 2024).

text.text: Understanding why creativity alters temporal experience may, thus, provide insight into the cognitive processes engaged during creative generation.
Here, we combine instructed sentence generation with prospective temporal production to investigate how the semantic demands of creativity relate to the processing and experience of time.
Creative generation involves balancing broad exploration of semantic space with the selection of contextually relevant representations (Beaty et al., 2023; Kenett, 2019; Ovando-Tellez et al., 2022).

text.text: Novelty requires moving beyond dominant semantic associations to access more remote possibilities, whereas appropriateness requires evaluating and selecting responses that remain relevant to the current context.
Behavioural measures such as semantic distance provide an objective index of semantic exploration by quantifying how far a response moves from dominant associations.

Complementary lexical and contextual measures can further characterize the accessibility and predictability of retrieved concepts (Benedek et al., 2017; Forthmann et al., 2016; Kenett & Faust, 2019; Weinstein et al., 2022).

text.text: At the same time, generating more remote responses involves overcoming highly accessible concepts and selecting weaker semantic representations (Beaty et al., 2017; Beaty & Kenett, 2023; Cassotti et al., 2016; Chrysikou, 2019; Luft et al., 2018; Zioga, Kenett, et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, creative generation involves coordinating associative exploration and controlled selection to move beyond dominant responses while preserving taskrelevant constraints.
Creative engagement can also alter how the passage of time is experienced.

Experimental work on flow has shown that moderate attentional demands can produce a subjective sense that time passes more quickly (Im & Varma, 2018), while others suggest that reduced attention to the passage of time contributes to this temporal acceleration (Lemmens et al., 2025; Rutrecht et al., 2021).

text.text: Similar distortions have been reported in creative and immersive activities, including musical performance, where performers describe losing awareness of time and where greater engagement in flow has been associated with altered temporal experience (Chirico et al., 2015; Droit-Volet et al., 2013; Gibbs & Schiavio, 2025; Wrigley & Emmerson, 2013; Zielke et al., 2023).

text.text: These findings suggest that altered temporal experience may emerge when attention becomes strongly engaged with an ongoing creative activity, but they do not establish the cognitive processes responsible for this experience.

In particular, it remains unclear whether temporal distortions are related to specific properties of the generative process itself, such as the expansion of semantic space or the demands associated with producing a response.
Furthermore, it is unclear whether any temporal effects are accompanied by autonomic changes that could provide an alternative explanation based on physiological arousal.
Moreover, temporal experience encompasses distinct components: online prospective duration tracking and post-trial subjective evaluations of time passage.
Whether these components are similarly affected by the demands of creative generation remains unclear.
This coordination can be experimentally probed by manipulating the instructions under which participants generate ideas.

Previous research has shown that explicit instructions to "be creative" enhance the originality of generated responses (Chen et al., 2005; Harrington, 1975; Niu & Liu, 2009; Nusbaum et al., 2014; Zioga et al., 2024), leading to distinct behavioural and physiological profiles relative to conventional or unconventional goals across expressive domains (language: Heinen & Johnson, 2018; music: Zioga et al., 2026).

text.text: Building on this approach, the present study uses instructed sentence generation to manipulate the demands of creative semantic processing.
Participants generated sentences in response to noun triplets under three instruction conditions: conventional, creative, and unconventional.
Conventionality encourages accessible and contextually-related responses.
Unconventionality instead encourages participants to depart from dominant associations and produce atypical responses.
Creativity combines these demands, requiring participants to move beyond typical associations while producing responses that remain meaningful and appropriate to the task.
To examine how these different configurations of cognitive demands relate to temporal processing, we combined instructed idea generation with prospective temporal production.
Participants generated sentences while concurrently tracking duration to produce a specified target interval (10 s or 20 s), executing a keypress when they judged the duration had elapsed.
Following each trial, they completed post-trial ratings assessing their subjective temporal accuracy and subjective passage of time.
Following the aforementioned literature, we hypothesize that the instruction conditions will produce dissociable semantic and contextual profiles reflecting the given demands.

Specifically, we used two planned orthogonal contrasts to distinguish a creative-specific effect from an effect of increasing unconventionality from conventional to creative to unconventional generation.

We expected semantic distance between prompts and responses to increase progressively from conventional to creative to unconventional conditions, reflecting increasing departure from the semantic context provided by the prompts.

Compared to conventional and unconventional conditions, we further expected creativity to exhibit greater within-response semantic range, reflecting a broader semantic space traversed during sentence construction.
Finally, we expected the conditions to differ in contextual uncertainty, indexed by entropy and surprisal, reflecting differences in the predictability of lexical choices.
We further hypothesized that creative generation would alter both prospective and subjective temporal processing.

Specifically, we expected creative generation to be associated with greater signed proportional error (i.e., temporal overproduction, where produced intervals exceed the target duration), consistent with reduced temporal pulse accumulation as executive resources are diverted away from temporal monitoring.
We also expected elevated absolute proportional error, indexing diminished temporal precision.
Crucially, we evaluated the coefficient of variation, predicting that proportional variance would remain preserved across conditions.
Concurrently, we hypothesized that creative generation would accelerate the post-trial subjective passage of time.

Finally, we hypothesized that greater within-response semantic range would be associated with greater signed proportional error, consistent with the possibility that broader semantic exploration contributes to variation in temporal processing.

We additionally examined whether creative generation, semantic trajectory dynamics, and temporal production were accompanied by modulations in autonomic activity, operationalized via heart rate and phasic electrodermal activity.

The final number of participants involved in the present study exceeded the a priori sample size (N = 28) estimated by means of a power analysis using G*Power (Faul et al., 2009; repeated-measures ANOVA, within-factors, f = 0.25, α = 0.05, 1-β = 0.80, 3 measurements, correlation among repeated measures = 0.50).

We combined instructed story generation adapted from Rastelli and colleagues (2025) with prospective temporal production in a dual-task paradigm (Figure 1A).

text.text: On each trial, participants were presented with a prompt word triplet and instructed to generate and articulate a single sentence (a short story) according to one of three experimental instructions: 1.
Conventional: Form a common, typical sentence using common semantic links and the first association that comes to mind; 2.
Creative: Produce an original, imaginative, and evocative sentence (akin to a poetic story) connecting all three words coherently; and 3.
Unconventional: Form an unorthodox sentence combining the words in an atypical manner that avoids standard semantic relationships.
Standardized examples were provided during initial instruction (e.g., blacksmith-boat-lemons; airplane-field-newspaper).
Prompt words could be inflected into any grammatical form.
The experiment comprised 6 blocks of 6 trials (36 trials total), preceded by a practice block.
Each trial presented the word triplet, the condition instruction, and a designated target interval to produce (10 s or 20 s to prevent expectancy effects; counterbalanced across conditions).
While generating and articulating their sentence, participants prospectively monitored time and pressed a designated response key when they judged the target duration had elapsed.

Stimuli were sampled across six categories (plants, occupations, artifacts, animals, locations, vehicles), with each triplet containing at most one word per category to prevent automatic categorical priming.

Stimuli were matched across four criteria: 1) Lexical frequency: Selected from the upper quartile (> 75th percentile) of log-transformed relative word frequencies in SUBTLEX-GR (Dimitropoulou et al., 2010); 2) Concreteness: Verified in the upper quartile (> 75th percentile) of normative concreteness ratings (Brysbaert et al., 2014); 3) Word length: Constrained between 2 and 5 syllables; and 4) Semantic distance: 300-dimensional static word embeddings confirmed that pairwise cosine similarities between prompt words within each triplet (word1-word2, word1-word3, word2-word3) did not differ significantly.

text.text: The 36 experimental triplets were distributed equally across the three instruction conditions (12 items per condition), with 6 practice triplets sampled at random per participant from the reserve set.
EDA and cardiac PPG were recorded continuously using an EmotiBit wireless sensor module (Montgomery et al., 2024) placed on the participant's non-dominant (left) hand.

text.text: Cardiac pulse waveforms were recorded via a three-wavelength reflective PPG sensor at 25 Hz, while EDA was sampled at 15 Hz from the same module.
Raw signals were logged locally to an onboard micro-SD card for offline artifact rejection and signal processing.
2.5 Data preprocessing and metric extraction 2.5.1 Physiological signal processing Electrodermal Activity (EDA).
Continuous EDA signals were resampled to 50 Hz and decomposed into tonic and phasic components using NeuroKit2.
Mean tonic skin conductance level (SCL) and mean phasic EDA were calculated across the complete trial window (stimulus onset to response keypress).
Phasic driver bursts and discrete peak onsets were detected with a standard slopeinflection algorithm (0.1 μS amplitude threshold).
Trials exhibiting sensor detachment or contact loss (mean SCL ≤ 0.05 μS) were excluded as artifacts.
Green-light PPG signals were resampled to 100 Hz, bandpass filtered, and processed using the Elgendi peak-detection and Kubios artifact-correction algorithms in NeuroKit2.
Mean heart rate (HR, in bpm) and the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD, indexing short-term pulse-rate variability) were computed across each trial.
Trials were excluded if mean HR fell outside 40-160 bpm, or if artifact rates exceeded 30% for HR or 20% (with fewer than six clean successive differences) for RMSSD.
Linguistic and semantic modeling.
Spoken utterances were transcribed using Gemini 3.6 flash, verified by an author, and processed with the Modern Greek spaCy pipeline (el_core_news_lg).
Non-target content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) were extracted after removing diacritics, punctuation, stopwords, and the three prompt words.
Missing or unintelligible recordings were discarded.

Speech onset latency, defined as the interval from stimulus presentation to vocal onset; and 2.
Speech duration, defined as the articulatory duration from vocal onset to completion.

Multiple comparisons were controlled using False Discovery Rate (FDR), applied across hypothesis tests; covariates (e.g., trial order, target duration) were excluded from correction.

To determine how instructions modulated semantic and contextual properties of verbal generation, separate LMMs were fitted across semantic distance mean and range (within-response and promptresponse), contextual language modeling (entropy and surprisal), and lexical frequency.
Fixed effects comprised the planned contrasts (C1, C2) and trial order.
Speech onset latency and speech duration were examined subsequently in exploratory analyses.

To test whether generative instructions were associated with prospective timing and subjective temporal experience, separate LMMs were fitted across the four trial-level timing outcomes: signed proportional error, absolute proportional error, the subjective passage of time, and subjective temporal accuracy.
Fixed effects included C1 and C2 contrasts and trial order.

Additionally, to examine scalar temporal variability across conditions, an LMM was fitted on the participant-by-condition aggregate coefficient of variation with fixed effects of C1 and C2 contrasts and a participant random intercept.

To evaluate whether temporal distortions were driven by high-level semantic search or lower-level motor articulation, we implemented a three-tier hierarchical LMM framework across completecase observations for the three primary timing outcomes (signed proportional error, absolute proportional error, and the subjective passage of time): 1.
Semantic process models: Timing outcomes were regressed on within-response semantic range, prompt-response semantic range, contextual entropy and surprisal, alongside C1 and C2, and trial order; 2.
Speech-production models: Timing outcomes were regressed on speech onset latency and speech duration alongside base task controls; and 3.
Integrated models and incremental validity: Semantic and speech predictors were entered simultaneously into full models.

Nested models were re-estimated using Maximum Likelihood (ML) to perform Likelihood Ratio Tests, testing whether speech dynamics accounted for incremental variance beyond semantic structure, and vice versa.
Final parameters were obtained using REML.

Following the exploratory regression analyses, we conducted a 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis to quantify the corresponding within-person indirect pathway using person-mean centering (Zhang et al., 2009).

The within-person indirect effect was evaluated using participant cluster bootstrapping (B = 1,000 resamples with replacement at the participant level) to compute asymmetric 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
Physiology was analyzed across a three-part LMM battery examining continuous EDA (tonic SCL, phasic EDA) and PPG (mean HR, RMSSD) over the full trial window (prompt onset to button press).
In addition to trial order, target duration (10 s vs. 20 s) was included as a covariate across all models: 1.
Instruction effects on physiological state: Physiological measures were regressed on C1, C2, trial order, and target interval; 2.

Predicting physiology from semantic and linguistic metrics: Separate LMMs tested whether semantic distance (mean and range within/prompt) or language modeling (entropy and surprisal) predicted physiology beyond speech production demands, adjusting for speech onset latency, speech duration, and base covariates; and 3.

Discussion In this study, we investigated how different modes of verbal generation relate to the processing and experience of time.
Participants generated sentences under conventional, creative, and unconventional instructions while electrodermal and cardiac signals were recorded.

Our findings reveal four key results: (1) Creative generation was characterized by broader semantic exploration while preserving contextual constraint; (2) Creative generation induced prospective interval overproduction, a distortion primarily mediated by the demands of prolonged speech articulation; (3) The subjective passage of time accelerated across both creative and unconventional trials, decoupling the perceived speed of time from interval overproduction (signed proportional error); and (4) Autonomic activity provided distinct signatures of generative effort and temporal pacing: tonic sympathetic effort indexed unconventional rule-breaking, while transient autonomic arousal (phasic EDA and heart rate) independently predicted prospective interval underproduction, consistent with an accelerated internal pacemaker.
Together, these findings indicate that temporal estimation during idea generation is shaped by both embodied articulatory demands and internal autonomic pacing.
One of our central findings was that creative generation increased the range of semantic distances within utterances and relative to prompt triads, without increasing average semantic distance.
Thus, creative responses spanned a wider range of semantic relations without becoming uniformly remote.

This distinction is theoretically important: while semantic distance captures the remoteness of an idea, creativity requires original elements to remain integrated within taskappropriate structural constraints (Beaty et al., 2023; Orwig et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024).

text.text: Contemporary frameworks conceptualize creative cognition not as unguided divergence, but as flexible associative search coupled with effective executive selection and semantic organization (Beaty et al., 2023; Rastelli et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023).

text.text: Our findings support this balance: creative generation reflects broad conceptual exploration that preserves both proximal and distal semantic relations.
Computational language modeling provided a complementary information-theoretic perspective on this dissociation.
Creative generation reduced contextual entropy, demonstrating that creative utterances preserved predictability and syntactic-contextual coherence despite their conceptual breadth.
Conversely, unconventional generation sharply increased both entropy and surprisal, reflecting heightened contextual uncertainty and local lexical unpredictability (Slaats & Martin, 2025).
text.formatted: Conversely, unconventional generation sharply increased both entropy and surprisal, reflecting heightened contextual uncertainty and local lexical unpredictability <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Slaats & Martin, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, the absence of condition differences in lexical frequency confirms that these effects were not consequences of selecting rarer words.
These findings, thus, demonstrate that creative generation achieves divergence through structured, low-uncertainty integration.
Balancing generative novelty with structural coherence has roots in empirical aesthetics and predictive processing accounts of cognition.

In particular, in Berlyne's (1971) classic psychobiological framework and the Wundt curve, aesthetic preference follows an inverted-U function where stimuli of intermediate novelty or complexity are preferred, whereas the extremely expected is experienced as dull and the extremely unexpected as jarring.

text.text: A similar principle plays also a big role in predictive processing models, in which cognitive engagement and aesthetic pleasure emerge from the dynamic tension between expectation and surprise (Cheung et al., 2019; Huron, 2006).

text.text: Extending this to creative production, Zioga and colleagues (2020) demonstrated that human evaluations of musical creativity follow an inverted-U relationship with statistical predictability: musical compositions that balance expected and unexpected musical intervals are judged as more creative than musical compositions that are either highly predictable or unpredictable.
These differing cognitive strategies were directly reflected in the dynamics of speech production.
Creative generation was marked by prolonged speech onset latencies and extended vocalization durations, whereas increasing unconventionality was accompanied by shorter vocalization duration.

Longer initiation and execution times are consistent with the heightened cognitive demands of retrieving, evaluating, and synthesizing distant semantic concepts into a coherent story (Acar et al., 2019), reflecting the increased control demands required during ruleguided word production (Zioga, Zhou, et al., 2024).

text.text: Creative generation induced an overproduction of target intervals alongside degradation in timing precision (elevated absolute temporal error).

These findings align with prospective timing accounts proposing that concurrent cognitive operations compete for limited executive resources (Balta et al., 2024; Brown, 2006; Brown & Merchant, 2007; Matthews & Meck, 2016).
text.formatted: These findings align with prospective timing accounts proposing that concurrent cognitive operations compete for limited executive resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Balta et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Brown, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Brown & Merchant, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Matthews & Meck, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When attention is directed toward an effortful generative task rather than temporal monitoring, the accumulation of internal temporal units may be slowed, resulting in longer physical intervals before the subjective target criterion is reached (Im & Varma, 2018; Lemmens et al., 2025; Rutrecht et al., 2021).
text.formatted: When attention is directed toward an effortful generative task rather than temporal monitoring, the accumulation of internal temporal units may be slowed, resulting in longer physical intervals before the subjective target criterion is reached <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Im & Varma, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Lemmens et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rutrecht et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, this prospective distortion was not a generic byproduct of divergent thinking: while creative generation produced pronounced overproduction and absolute proportional error, unconventional generation showed no signed proportional error and actually enhanced temporal precision.
Divergence achieved through rule-breaking, therefore, permitted stable temporal monitoring, whereas creative synthesis severely compromised prospective control.
Crucially, the observed elevation in trial-level absolute error was not accompanied by detectable differences in relative temporal variability.
Analysis of the coefficient of variation revealed no significant condition effect.

This distinction is informative because absolute proportional error indexes departure from the physical target duration, whereas the coefficient of variation indexes trial-to-trial dispersion relative to the participant's own mean production.
These findings are therefore compatible with creative generation inducing systematic overproduction rather than an increase in proportional variability.
These results indicate that the reduction in target precision during creative production was driven by consistent overproduction rather than noisy or disorganized timing.

Although broader within-response semantic exploration was positively associated with temporal overproduction in isolation, this relationship entirely disappeared once speech production dynamics were considered.
Speech onset latency and, most prominently, speech duration accounted for substantially more variance in temporal production and precision than semantic or contextual metrics alone.

Our within-person mediation model clarified the direction of this shared variance: trials requiring broader conceptual search demanded longer vocalization durations, which carried prospective productions past the target duration.

Because these dynamics were observational at the trial level, this pathway reflects a process rather than purely causal mediation: the executive overhead of retrieving and organizing distant semantic concepts manifests directly in prolonged motor articulation, which in turn stretches the produced temporal interval.

Importantly, speech execution did not fully exhaust the relationship between creativity and time: the creative contrast retained a significant direct effect on interval overproduction even after controlling for semantic distance, contextual entropy, onset latency, and speech duration.

This residual effect indicates that creative synthesis entails cognitive or mnemonic processes, such as ongoing evaluative monitoring, selection among competing candidates, or post-retrieval verification, that divert executive attention from temporal tracking independently of overt speech output.

Conversely, the precision-enhancing effect of unconventionality survived adjustment for speech dynamics, demonstrating that departing from dominant prompt-response associations does not compromise prospective interval tracking the way creative synthesis does.
Our findings demonstrate a clear dissociation between prospective duration production and the subjective passage of time.

While creative generation produced pronounced temporal overproduction and elevated absolute proportional error, unconventional generation yielded no signed proportional error and actually sharpened precision.

Nevertheless, participants reported that time passed significantly faster during both creative and unconventional trials than during conventional ones, an acceleration that was particularly prominent during creative generation.

This dissociation aligns with contemporary accounts distinguishing prospective duration production from subjective passage of time judgments, which can be differentially influenced by the ongoing cognitive and affective context (Lamprou et al., 2024; Martinelli & Droit-Volet, 2022).
text.formatted: This dissociation aligns with contemporary accounts distinguishing prospective duration production from subjective passage of time judgments, which can be differentially influenced by the ongoing cognitive and affective context <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lamprou et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Martinelli & Droit-Volet, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas prospective interval production depends on continuous attentional monitoring to determine when a chronometric criterion has elapsed, passage of time evaluations are post-trial, subjective appraisals shaped primarily by task engagement, absorption, and perceived cognitive effort.
Our results extend this distinction to active language generation, showing that the subjective impression of time "flying" can occur independently of directional distortions in interval production.
This decoupling was further corroborated at the trial level by our continuous predictor models.
While semantic exploration metrics and speech production dynamics were strong predictors of directional temporal overproduction, neither accounted for variation in subjective passage of time.

The unconventional condition provides a compelling illustration of this divergence: despite exhibiting narrower internal semantic range, greater local surprisal, and significantly shorter speech production than creative trials, unconventional generation accelerated subjective passage just as robustly, without biasing interval production.
This pattern indicates that subjective acceleration reflects absorption in the act of generative problem-solving rather than the specific articulatory or attentional bottlenecks that distort timing.

Consistent with flow and absorption accounts (Rutrecht et al., 2021), high immersion in an effortful generative task reduces meta-awareness of time's passage, speeding its perceived transit even while the underlying interval-production mechanisms remain accurately calibrated.

text.text: Prospective chronometric timing and subjective temporal experience, thus, capture functionally independent dimensions of creative cognition.
Peripheral autonomic dynamics revealed distinct physiological signatures for creative versus unconventional generation.
Creative generation was characterized by attenuated phasic EDA, and greater within-response mean semantic distance was similarly associated with lower phasic EDA.

Electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that accessing remote semantic concepts requires the active inhibition of obvious, habitual associations, a process supported by temporal alpha band oscillations (Luft et al., 2018; Zioga, Kenett, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that accessing remote semantic concepts requires the active inhibition of obvious, habitual associations, a process supported by temporal alpha band oscillations <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Luft et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Zioga, Kenett, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As phasic EDA typically reflects externally directed attention and orienting responses, engaging in internally focused semantic retrieval likely attenuates these transient sympathetic responses.
In contrast, increasing unconventionality was accompanied by elevated tonic SCL.

Given that tonic SCL indexes sustained sympathetic tone associated with cognitive effort and preparatory mobilization, this elevation aligns with the greater executive control required to actively suppress dominant associations (Beaty et al., 2014 (Beaty et al., , 2017;; Zioga, Kenett, et al., 2024).

text.text: Autonomic dynamics, thus, suggest a double dissociation: creative generation relies on internally directed associative expansion, whereas unconventionality demands sustained executive inhibition.
Furthermore, autonomic arousal served as a direct pacemaker for prospective interval production.
Both elevated phasic EDA and higher heart rate were associated with shorter produced intervals.
This pattern is consistent with pacemaker-accumulator models of timing (Arslanova et al., 2023; Cellini et al., 2015; Fung et al., 2017; Sadeghi et al., 2023; Volodina et al., 2025).

text.text: According to these frameworks, heightened sympathetic tone and elevated cardiac chronotropy accelerate the emission rate of an internal pacemaker.

Because temporal pulses accumulate more rapidly during states of higher autonomic arousal, the subjective criterion representing the target interval is reached in less physical time, resulting in compressed interval productions.

These findings converge with physiological timing paradigms demonstrating that elevated sympathetic tone and physical exertion consistently produce relative interval underproduction (Davis et al., 2026; Fung et al., 2017; Lamprou et al., 2025; Volodina et al., 2025).

text.text: Critically, neither phasic EDA nor heart rate predicted the subjective passage of time, reinforcing the dissociation of prospective production and subjective temporal experience.

Whereas prospective production is an online chronometric task directly modulated by visceral arousal and pulse accumulation, subjective passage of time evaluations are higher-order appraisals shaped primarily by task absorption, valence, and cognitive engagement (Micillo et al., 2026; Ogden et al., 2022).

text.text: Our findings align with ambulatory and laboratory evidence showing that autonomic fluctuations exert negligible influence on subjective passage of time judgments in the absence of explicit affective threat cues (Micillo et al., 2026; Ogden et al., 2019 Ogden et al., , 2022;; Piovesan et al., 2019).

text.text: Autonomic arousal, thus, acts specifically as a somatic pacemaker for metric interval tracking, leaving the phenomenological feeling of time's passage unaffected.
Our findings demonstrate that creative generation leads to prospective temporal overproduction and impaired temporal precision, while accelerating the subjective passage of time.

Importantly, creative generation elicits a distinct computational and physiological profile, characterized by high within-response semantic range alongside low contextual uncertainty, reflecting a balance between conceptual divergence and structural coherence, as well as reduced phasic electrodermal activity.

The results further demonstrate that creative overproduction is mediated by prolonged speech duration, indicating that semantic search shapes prospective timing through the embodied demands of speech production, while, in line with internal pacemaker accounts, elevated heart rate and phasic EDA predict shorter produced intervals.
Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal experience during creative thought is governed by a dynamic interplay between embodied speech production demands and autonomic state.

Within-response mean semantic distance: Average pairwise cosine distance among all produced content lemmas; 2.
